L1-01.why: GUESS. Four full sentences, no stem. Eliminated nothing on structure; picked C because it is the only one that reframes the atlas's audience (a typical paragraph-to-paragraph pivot), while B and D are anecdote-shaped. Essentially a coin flip among A/B/C/D.

L1-02.why: Dangling-modifier cast, decidable from options alone. 'Wrapped in string or sheepskin' must attach to a noun that can be wrapped. A attaches it to 'it' (expletive), D to 'carrying'. Only B puts 'the graphite sticks' in subject position. C is No Change and the presence of two distinct dangling rewrites implies the original dangles too.

L1-03.why: Yes/No rhetorical-purpose item. A and D are killed on false premises (nothing else suggests a country-by-country comparison or a travelers' history). Real contest is B vs C, which disagree about whether the science is background or the bulk. Chose C because 'explains how the sound is produced' is the likelier shape of a booming-dunes passage and C's 'briefly at the end' is the more modest claim. Partly a guess between two survivors.

L1-04.why: Pure redundancy cast, decidable without the passage. A ('good drill of high quality') and B ('good and of high quality') say the same thing twice; C is No Change. D is the only concise option and the shortest. Classic ACT concision item.

L1-05.why: GUESS, weakly steered. Rhetorical-function options. D is a negation-shaped distractor ('customers still preferred the grandmother's'), B reads as a deflating alternate reading, C claims a paragraph-1 condition I cannot verify. A is the straightforward affirming reading (narrator's work indistinguishable from grandmother's), which is the usual key shape for a closing detail. No real evidence.

L1-06.why: GUESS. Sentence-choice item with no stem. B ('The markers were the trouble') is too thin to be a key; A and C are both specific. Picked C because a general statement about the breakwater failing is the likelier topic-sentence/transition function, but this is near-random and D (No Change) is live.

L1-07.why: GUESS among transitions. 'meanwhile' (D) is a weak contrast/time word rarely keyed; 'for example' vs 'so' is the real contest. Chose 'so' on the physical reading that a swept stone is the RESULT of the sweeping mechanism just described, not an illustration of a category. Could easily be A.

L1-08.why: GUESS. Sentence-placement item, four positions, no passage. Slight prior against 'where it is now' (B) since placement items usually relocate. Chose 'beginning of the paragraph' over 'after the first sentence' on no evidence at all. 1-in-3 at best.

L1-09.why: Decidable from options. Subject is singular ('the [X] of the wheel'), so 'were' (B) fails agreement; 'being' (C) makes a fragment; D inserts a comma between subject and verb. The remaining well-formed reading is 'wheel was that it would', which must be No Change (A). Small residual risk that the original has some other flaw not visible in the fragment.

L1-10.why: GUESS. Word-choice among 'considers / inspects / notices' plus No Change. These differ in meaning and the passage decides; nothing in the option set discriminates. Defaulted to No Change because three near-synonymous substitutes with no concision or register difference is the shape of a No Change item.

L1-11.why: Apostrophe cast, fully decidable blind. A has a false plural apostrophe ('arm's'), D has 'its'' which is not a word. C is the clean possessive 'its two arms is'. B (No Change) is excluded because the two error options bracket exactly the error being tested.

L1-12.why: Conjunctive-adverb punctuation, decidable blind. 'however' joining two independent clauses needs a semicolon before and comma after. A has no punctuation before, B splices with a comma, D is No Change (presumably one of those errors). C is the only correctly punctuated form.

L1-13.why: GUESS, effectively random. 'Point A/B/C/D' with no passage carries zero information. Chose 'Point C' on the weak heuristic that interior insertion points are keyed more often than the first or last.

L1-14.why: Weak. Rhetorical-function options. A leans on the absolute 'the one obstacle'; D is a strained 'concession' framing; C and B both describe a contrast but B's cross-reference (para 4, how new audio dramas are made) is the more ordinary essay move. Picked B mainly on the distractor-absolutism tell, not on knowledge.

L1-15.why: Register cast, visible in the options alone: A is too colloquial ('cracking up big time'), B is comically inflated ('emitted an audible expression of amusement'), leaving the neutral 'laughed out loud'. Risk is that No Change (D) is already neutral and C is a pointless swap, which is why this is not higher.
